first.rationale: The competitor's entry pricing makes promotional_pricing the tempting move, but memory_73 is explicit that it bought acquisition at the cost of 30-day retention and should not be generalized; that trades directly against the primary objective of sustainable long-term qualified revenue, so I decline it despite the immediate pressure. The two internal metrics actually degrading are onboarding completion (-4%) and activation (-6%), and these are causally linked: onboarding completion is upstream of activation, so a fix there plausibly moves both, whereas activation messaging treats the downstream symptom only. memory_86 (onboarding shortening lifted completion and time-to-value across self-serve) and memory_31 (signup field reduction produced a durable first-week activation lift) converge on this direction, and 'durable' in memory_31 is the quality I care about. I spend verification on memory_86 because it is the load-bearing evidence for my chosen action and I want the original record's effect size, sample, and whether the lift held past week one, and on memory_91 because activation_messaging is the strongest alternative and I want to know if its week-one engagement gain was a real behavior change or a transient nudge before I forgo it. Note these are consolidated summaries, not raw results: memory_86 and memory_31 may be partly the same underlying finding double-counted, and neither tells me whether the earlier lifts were measured under competitive pressure like today's. Downstream value risk: cutting signup or onboarding fields can strip qualification data used by sales routing and by enterprise pipeline scoring (memory_44's demo-request path), so a completion-rate win could quietly degrade lead quality and thus *qualified* revenue. I therefore run this as a standard experiment with lead-quality and 30-day retention as guardrail metrics alongside completion, not just a completion-rate readout, and I will revisit if verification shows memory_86's lift did not persist.

mid.rationale: Verification came back clean and it sharpened rather than merely confirmed the choice. exp_86 shows completion +13%, time-to-value -2.1 days, and critically 30-day retention +3% — the onboarding win is not a vanity-metric win, it moves the retention term that actually determines sustainable qualified revenue. exp_91 is also real (activation +6%, retention +1%) and I want to be honest that it is a genuinely good option I am declining, not a strawman; I decline it because onboarding completion sits upstream of activation, so fixing completion plausibly recovers part of the -6% activation gap as well, while activation messaging cannot recover the -4% completion gap. On the margins exp_86 dominates on retention (+3% vs +1%) and addresses both degraded metrics rather than one. I continue to refuse promotional_pricing despite the competitor's entry pricing: memory_73 is explicit that its acquisition lift came with a material 30-day retention loss, and buying price-sensitive accounts that churn is precisely the failure mode the primary objective rules out. enterprise_sales_assist (memory_44) is unrelated to the two metrics that are actually degrading and is unverified. One correction from the archive that changes my execution: exp_86 tested a shortened onboarding flow, not signup field reduction. memory_31's signup-field claim remains unverified and I am no longer treating the two as interchangeable evidence for one intervention — I will replicate the verified intervention (shorten the post-signup onboarding flow) and will NOT strip qualification fields at signup. That scoping also largely defuses the downstream risk I flagged: cutting signup fields would degrade the qualification data that sales routing and the memory_44 demo-request path depend on, converting a completion win into a quiet loss in lead quality and therefore in *qualified* revenue. Residual uncertainty I am carrying rather than hiding: exp_86 ran under different conditions than today's competitive pressure, its effect size may not replicate against a competitor actively pulling SMB accounts, and the archive gave no sample size or duration. I run this as a standard experiment, not a broad rollout, with 30-day retention and downstream lead-quality/pipeline metrics as explicit guardrails alongside completion and activation, and I hold the promotional-pricing question open as a separately-scoped, retention-guarded question rather than letting competitive urgency override memory_73.

final2.rationale: The new information is real and it hurts, but it does not change what the evidence supports. A deeper competitor cut and doubled churn conversations increase the URGENCY of a response; they do not supply any new evidence that promotional_pricing WORKS. The only record I have on that direction is memory_73, which says the lift came with a material 30-day retention loss and explicitly warns against generalizing it. Discounting into a price war against a competitor who can cut again next week means buying back the least durable accounts at a permanently lower price point — that is the exact opposite of maximizing sustainable long-term qualified revenue, and it is the decision I would most regret in a quarter. I want to be explicit about one thing I cannot resolve: memory_73 tested promotional pricing for ACQUISITION of price-sensitive SMB accounts, whereas today's pressure is defensive RETENTION of existing accounts. Those are not the same intervention, and I do not know that memory_73's retention harm transfers to the defensive case — but I equally do not know that its revenue lift transfers. My budget is spent, so that question is genuinely unverified in both directions, and 'unverified' under leadership pressure is not a license to assume the favorable half. I am not going to spend the single non-carrying slot on the one direction my memory carries an explicit warning about, on the strength of an extrapolation I cannot check. So I hold: replicate the verified exp_86 intervention — shorten the post-signup onboarding flow. It is the only candidate that is verified, that moves BOTH degraded metrics (completion -4%, activation -6%, with completion upstream of activation), and that improved 30-day retention (+3%). Retention is precisely the currency at risk this week, which makes onboarding a real, if slower, answer to churn rather than a refusal to answer. I keep the correction from the archive: exp_86 shortened the onboarding flow, it did not strip signup fields. memory_31's signup-field claim stays unverified, so I will not cut qualification fields at signup — that would degrade sales routing and the memory_44 demo-request pipeline and turn a completion win into a loss in QUALIFIED revenue, the risk I flagged earlier. Guardrails unchanged and now more important: 30-day retention, lead quality, and pipeline alongside completion and activation, run as a standard experiment rather than a broad rollout because exp_86's effect size was measured without this competitive pressure and may not fully replicate. Separately and outside this experiment slot, the right response to doubled churn conversations is direct account work — talk to the at-risk accounts, understand whether the driver is price or unrealized value — and to scope defensive pricing as its own retention-guarded question for next week's archive budget. That is a real response to leadership today; it is just not a reason to spend the experiment slot on the intervention my own record warns against.
